title: The exile (2 Kings 25)
hookLine: Jerusalem falls in 587 BC and the Temple burns

lines: THE TEMPLE THAT WAS FILLED WITH CLOUD.
cards: Last week, a cloud filled Solomon's Temple. Today it burns. Kings has warned of this for chapters: king after king turning away, prophet after prophet calling them back.
Now the army of Babylon surrounds Jerusalem, under King Nebuchadnezzar, Nabuchodonosor in the Douay-Rheims. The siege drags on from the ninth year of the king into the eleventh. The food runs out.
The text says it in one line: there was no bread for the people of the land. Then the walls are breached, in 587 BC by one common reckoning, and the last king of Judah runs for it in the night.

teach.h: THE LAST KING OF JUDAH, BLINDED.
teach.b: 2 Kings tells it with almost no comment, which makes it worse. King Zedekiah, Sedecias in the Douay, is caught near Jericho.
His sons are killed in front of him, then his eyes are put out, so that this is the last thing he sees.

teach.h: THE HOUSE OF THE LORD BURNS.
teach.b: The next month the Babylonian commander arrives, and the Douay says simply: "he burnt the house of the Lord, and the king's house, and the houses of Jerusalem." The walls are pulled down.
The people are marched off to Babylon, far to the east. Only the poorest are left behind to tend the vines and fields. Exile means more than moving.

It means losing the land God promised, the king from David's line, and the Temple where God chose to dwell, all at once. Some scholars think much of the Hebrew Bible took its final shape in its shadow.
Back on day one hundred eighty-nine came the psalm of the exiles, Psalm one thirty-six in the Douay: "Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept: when we remembered Sion."
And their question: "How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a strange land?" Now it's clear why they wept. But listen to how 2 Kings ends.

teach.h: A SEAT AT THE KING'S TABLE.
teach.b: Decades later, a new king of Babylon lets David's descendant, Jehoiachin, out of prison, speaks kindly to him, and gives him a seat at his table for the rest of his life.

teach.h: HOW SHALL WE SING IN A STRANGE LAND?
teach.b: A small, strange thread of hope. The line of David isn't finished.

how: Catholics hear the fall of Jerusalem in the Mass readings, pray Psalm 137 (136 in the Douay) on the Fourth Sunday of Lent in one year of the cycle, and the Church remembers the Holy Family's flight into Egypt when it speaks of care for migrants and refugees.

being forced away from your homeland
a prison sentence in a foreign city

games.q: the fall of Jerusalem — tap the pairs.
p: king of Babylon who besieged the city
the last king of Judah, blinded
left behind to tend the vines

s: every person in Judah was taken to Babylon
the poorest were left behind as vinedressers and farmers.
2 Kings ends with a small sign of hope
David's descendant is freed from prison and eats at the king's table.
the exiles' psalm is set in Jerusalem
it is set by the rivers of Babylon, remembering Zion.

games.q: you're an exile by the rivers of Babylon. your captors ask you to sing one of the songs of Zion for them. what do you do?
o: sing it, to keep the peace.
hang up your harp and weep.
make up a new song for Babylon.
games.why: the psalm says they hung their instruments on the willows: how shall we sing the song of the Lord in a strange land?

practice: Think of people far from where they belong right now: refugees crossing borders, families whose homes burned or flooded, someone sleeping in a car, maybe someone in your own life who had to leave everything.

Picture them sitting by strange waters, remembering home. If you pray, hold them before God and ask for what they most need; if you don't, let yourself feel their loss for a moment without looking away.

wordCard.voice: Exile. Being forced from your homeland; for Judah, the fall of Jerusalem, the burning of the Temple, and the long years in Babylon. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: exile, captivity. In later Jewish thought, galut also names the long condition of living away from the land.

carryVoice: Your line: by the waters again. Even here, a small thread of hope. Until tomorrow.
